learningObjectives.title: Nazi control and the police state
Life for different groups in society
Persecution, the Holocaust and wartime Germany

questions.q: Who was the overall leader of the SS in Nazi Germany?
options: Heinrich Himmler
Joseph Goebbels
Ernst Röhm
Hermann Göring
questions.explain: Heinrich Himmler led the SS, which grew into the most powerful instrument of the Nazi police state.

questions.q: What was the role of the Gestapo?
options: The Nazi secret state police
The Nazi youth movement for boys
The state propaganda ministry
The regular uniformed traffic police
questions.explain: The Gestapo was the secret state police, tasked with hunting out opponents of the regime.

questions.q: In which year did the Night of the Long Knives take place?
questions.explain: The purge of the SA leadership occurred in June 1934, removing a rival threat to Hitler's power.

questions.q: Why did Hitler order the Night of the Long Knives?
options: To remove the threat posed by the SA and its leader Ernst Röhm
To take over the Catholic Church in Germany
To begin the mass deportation of Jews
To end unemployment among young men
questions.explain: Hitler eliminated Röhm and the SA leadership to secure army support and remove rivals within the party.

questions.q: Where was the first Nazi concentration camp, opened in 1933, located?
options: Dachau
Auschwitz
Belsen
Treblinka
questions.explain: Dachau opened in 1933 to hold political prisoners and was run by the SS.

questions.q: A factory worker quietly criticises Hitler to a workmate and is arrested by the Gestapo a few days later. What does this best show about the police state?
options: The Gestapo relied heavily on ordinary people informing on one another
The Gestapo had enough officers to watch every citizen directly
Criticism of Hitler was legally permitted but discouraged
The SA carried out most arrests of ordinary workers
questions.explain: The Gestapo was relatively small and depended on a network of informers and denunciations to create a climate of fear.

questions.q: Who was the Nazi Minister of Propaganda?
options: Joseph Goebbels
Reinhard Heydrich
Baldur von Schirach
Robert Ley
questions.explain: Goebbels controlled propaganda, using radio, film, newspapers and rallies to spread Nazi ideas.

questions.q: Why was Pastor Martin Niemöller and the Confessional Church a problem for the Nazis?
options: They resisted Nazi attempts to control and reshape the Protestant Church
They demanded that Germany rearm more quickly
They supported the Communist Party against Hitler
They organised the assassination of leading Nazis
questions.explain: The Confessional Church opposed Nazi interference in religion, and Niemöller was eventually imprisoned in a concentration camp.

questions.q: Which slogan summed up the Nazi view of a woman's ideal role?
options: Kinder, Küche, Kirche (children, kitchen, church)
Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer
Blood and Soil
Strength Through Joy
questions.explain: Nazis wanted women to focus on children, the home and the church rather than careers or politics.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the marriage loans introduced under the Law for the Encouragement of Marriage (1933)?
options: To encourage 'racially fit' couples to marry and have more children
To reduce the number of women working in factories only
To provide housing for unemployed men
To fund rearmament of the German army
questions.explain: Loans were partly cancelled for each child born, aiming to raise the birth rate among approved Germans.

questions.q: What was the name of the Nazi youth organisation for girls?
options: The League of German Maidens (BDM)
The German Labour Front
The Hitler Youth (for girls only)
The Strength Through Joy movement
questions.explain: The Bund Deutscher Mädel prepared girls for their future roles as wives and mothers.

questions.q: What was a key aim of the Hitler Youth for boys?
options: To prepare them physically and ideologically for future military service
To train them as factory managers
To give them a broad, questioning academic education
To recruit them into the Confessional Church
questions.explain: Activities stressed fitness, discipline, Nazi ideology and military-style skills to ready boys for the armed forces.

questions.q: What did the 'Strength Through Joy' (Kraft durch Freude) scheme provide for workers?
options: Cheap leisure activities such as holidays and outings
Higher wages and the right to strike
Free university education
Land to farm in eastern Europe
questions.explain: KdF offered subsidised trips, sport and entertainment to keep workers loyal and content.

questions.q: Why did the Nazis reform school subjects such as History and Biology?
options: To indoctrinate pupils with Nazi ideas about race and German greatness
To prepare all pupils equally for university
To reduce the influence of the army on education
To encourage independent criticism of the government
questions.explain: Lessons were rewritten to teach racial theory, nationalism and loyalty to Hitler.

questions.q: A qualified German woman is dismissed from her post as a doctor soon after 1933. Which Nazi attitude best explains this?
options: Belief that women should leave professional careers for home and family
Belief that Germany had too few doctors overall
A shortage of hospitals in Germany
A policy of promoting women into senior government roles
questions.explain: Nazis pushed many women out of professions such as medicine, law and the civil service to prioritise motherhood.

questions.q: What were the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 primarily concerned with?
options: Removing Jewish citizenship and banning marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Setting up the first death camps
Banning all Christian churches
Introducing conscription into the army
questions.explain: The 1935 laws stripped Jews of Reich citizenship and forbade marriage or relations with 'Aryan' Germans.

questions.q: What was significant about Kristallnacht in November 1938?
options: It marked an escalation into widespread, organised violence against Jews
It was the first day of the Second World War
It was when the Nuremberg Laws were passed
It was the closure of all concentration camps
questions.explain: The 'Night of Broken Glass' saw synagogues, homes and shops attacked, and thousands of Jews arrested, intensifying persecution.

questions.q: Besides Jews, which of these groups was also persecuted by the Nazis as 'undesirable'?
options: Roma and Sinti (Gypsies)
Members of the army
Owners of Volkswagen cars
Workers in the German Labour Front
questions.explain: Nazis persecuted many groups, including Roma and Sinti, disabled people, homosexuals and political opponents.

questions.q: A wartime document from January 1942 records senior officials meeting to coordinate the 'Final Solution' across Europe. Which event does this describe?
options: The Wannsee Conference
The Nuremberg Rally
The Munich Putsch
The Night of the Long Knives
questions.explain: At Wannsee in January 1942, Nazi officials organised the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

questions.q: A German student group secretly distributes leaflets in 1943 urging people to resist Hitler, and its members are executed. Which group does this describe?
options: The White Rose
The Hitler Youth
The German Labour Front
The Einsatzgruppen
questions.explain: The White Rose, including Sophie and Hans Scholl, distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and were executed for resistance.
